clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in FKRP (fukutin-related protein); a common founder variant (L276I) predominates in Northern European populations and typically produces a milder, later-onset limb-girdle phenotype.
Belongs to the secondary dystroglycanopathies — hypoglycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan impairs its binding to laminin in the muscle basement membrane.
Proximal limb-girdle weakness with prominent calf (and sometimes tongue and thigh) hypertrophy; the phenotype can closely mimic Becker or Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are common and may be disproportionate to limb weakness, so both warrant systematic lifelong surveillance.
Serum creatine kinase is characteristically markedly elevated.
Exertional myalgia, cramps and myoglobinuria can occur and are sometimes the presenting feature.

Allelic severity spectrum: the same gene causes severe congenital muscular dystrophy (MDC1C) and structural brain and eye malformation syndromes (muscle-eye-brain disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome) at the severe end.
Muscle immunostaining shows reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan with a preserved protein core; secondary reduction of laminin-alpha2 may also be seen.
reference.pathophysiology: FKRP encodes fukutin-related protein, a ribitol-phosphate transferase acting in the Golgi apparatus during the post-translational glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Alpha-dystroglycan is a central element of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex that anchors the subsarcolemmal cytoskeleton to laminin-211 in the extracellular matrix. Loss of transferase activity shortens the functional matriglycan chain so that alpha-dystroglycan can no longer bind laminin, weakening the mechanical link across the sarcolemma. The resulting membrane fragility permits contraction-induced injury, myofibre necrosis and repeated cycles of regeneration that are eventually outpaced, with progressive replacement of muscle by fibrofatty tissue. The degree of residual glycosylation broadly correlates with clinical severity, explaining the wide spectrum from adult limb-girdle weakness to congenital brain and eye malformation.
additionalDifferentials: Other dystroglycanopathies (POMT1, POMT2, fukutin or GMPPB-related limb-girdle dystrophy)
Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (given raised creatine kinase and myalgia)
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing — FKRP sequencing or a next-generation neuromuscular gene panel, with targeted analysis for the common founder variant
Muscle biopsy with immunostaining and immunoblot for glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan and laminin-alpha2
Muscle MRI to define the pattern of selective involvement (posterior thigh, adductors, gastrocnemius)
Cardiac assessment with echocardiography and electrocardiography, and cardiac MRI where available
Respiratory assessment including erect and supine forced vital capacity and overnight oximetry with capnography
redFlags: New or progressive breathlessness, orthopnoea or morning headache suggesting respiratory muscle failure and nocturnal hypoventilation
Symptoms of heart failure or arrhythmia
Pigmented urine (myoglobinuria) after exertion or intercurrent illness, with risk of acute kidney injury
Peri-operative and anaesthetic risk, including avoidance of triggering agents and risk of rhabdomyolysis
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: the common founder genotype often permits ambulation into adulthood with slowly progressive weakness, whereas severe genotypes lead to earlier loss of walking. Cardiac and respiratory complications are the principal determinants of morbidity and mortality and are potentially treatable when detected early.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as Becker or Duchenne muscular dystrophy because of calf hypertrophy and a raised creatine kinase.
Overlooking cardiomyopathy or nocturnal hypoventilation because limb weakness appears comparatively mild.
Assuming a normal dystrophin stain excludes the diagnosis — specific glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan staining is required.
Attributing exertional myoglobinuria to a metabolic myopathy and missing the underlying dystroglycanopathy.
Expecting intellectual disability — cognition is typically normal in the limb-girdle phenotype, in contrast with the severe congenital forms.
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; management is supportive within a specialist neuromuscular multidisciplinary team

Systematic lifelong cardiac surveillance for dilated cardiomyopathy with echocardiography, ECG and cardiac MRI, treating established disease with standard heart-failure therapy such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers
Respiratory surveillance with erect and supine forced vital capacity and overnight oximetry with capnography, introducing non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy with orthoses and mobility aids, and counselling to maintain hydration and avoid triggers during episodes of exertional myalgia, cramps and myoglobinuria
Orthopaedic and spinal monitoring for contractures and scoliosis
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, noting the milder later-onset course typical of the common L276I founder variant
Escalate to advanced heart-failure care and assisted ventilation as cardiac or respiratory failure progresses
